where: Section 1 (process form of the first law)
problem: The chapter states the closed-system first law only as Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = U₂ − U₁. The general textbook form also carries the changes of kinetic and potential energy of the system as a whole: Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE. A student meeting a moving piston or a falling mass problem can wrongly apply the shorter form.
fix: Add one line: this form assumes the system is at rest and its centre of mass does not change height (ΔKE = 0, ΔPE = 0); when the whole system speeds up or rises, use Q₁₂ − W₁₂ = (U₂ − U₁) + (KE₂ − KE₁) + (PE₂ − PE₁).

problem: "Two different paths between the same states enclose different areas" is misleading. A given pair of paths encloses one fixed area; what differs is the area under each curve. Only the difference of those two areas, W_A − W_B, is the enclosed area.
fix: Write: each path has its own area under it on the p-V diagram, so W differs from path to path, and the area between the two paths equals W_A − W_B, the difference in work.

problem: Two loose claims. CFD codes solve the differential conservation equations (mass, momentum, energy) over each control volume; they do not solve δQ − δW = dU cell by cell. A battery pack's heat out equals electrical work in only when its stored internal energy is unchanged.
fix: Say that CFD codes solve the differential energy equation per control volume, which is the same first-law balance written for a tiny cell; and that for a battery, electrical work in = rise in stored energy + heat out, so heat out equals work in only when the stored energy does not change.
